opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the most interesting open questions right now, and I don't think anyone has fully figured it out. I find it useful to look at how we've handled this before. With credit cards, consumers got strong protections, like chargebacks and fraud liability caps. That shifted the risk onto the issuers and merchants, and that's a big part of why people became comfortable paying with a card online at all. Trust came first, and adoption followed.

With agents it gets messier, because there are more parties in the chain. There's you, the user. There's whoever built the agent, the model provider underneath it, the merchant, and the payment network. When something goes wrong, you have to ask what kind of wrong it was. Did the agent do exactly what you told it, and you just gave a bad instruction? Did it misread your intent? Did it get manipulated by something it saw on a website, like a prompt injection? Each of those feels like it should land on a different party.

My instinct is that risk should sit with whoever is best positioned to prevent the failure. If the agent was tricked by a malicious page, that's arguably on the agent developer to have built better guardrails. If you explicitly approved a purchase and later regretted it, that's probably on you, same as today. The hard cases are the ambiguous middle, where the agent did something "reasonable" that you never would have done.

Practically, I think we'll see a few things. One is scoped permissions: spending limits, merchant allowlists, and confirmation steps above a certain threshold, so the blast radius is bounded. Another is much better audit trails, so that after the fact you can actually reconstruct why the agent made a decision. You can't assign liability fairly if you can't explain what happened. And I suspect we'll eventually get something like insurance or guarantees from the platforms themselves. For mainstream users to hand over their wallet, someone credible has to say, "if this goes sideways, we've got you."

Until that exists, I'd expect most people to keep a human in the loop for anything consequential. That's fine, honestly. It's how trust gets built incrementally.

r001.rationale: The response discusses developer guardrails, platform insurance or guarantees, and card issuer/merchant protections, but does not identify accountability of a payment provider for an agent’s mistakes as a source of trust.

r002.rationale: It describes unresolved ambiguous cases and says users will likely keep a human involved for consequential actions, indicating that safeguards and trust measures leave residual risk.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that the current frameworks were not built for this, and everyone is kind of improvising. The way payments work today, the whole system of liability is built around the idea that there's a human who authorized a transaction, and the question is just whether that authorization was legitimate. Was it really you, was it fraud, did the merchant deliver what they promised. All of that assumes a person made a decision at the moment of payment.

When you have an agent making the payment, that assumption breaks in a few different ways. The person may have authorized the agent in general terms, like "book me a flight to Denver under five hundred dollars," but they didn't authorize this specific transaction with this specific merchant at this specific price. So who's on the hook if the agent books the wrong day? Or gets tricked by a merchant page that's been crafted to manipulate it? Or spends way more than you intended because it misunderstood the instruction?

My view is that in the long run, the risk needs to sit with whoever is in the best position to prevent the failure. And that's mostly not the end user. The user is the least equipped party here. They can't see what's happening inside the model, they can't audit the agent's reasoning, and they often won't even know something went wrong until the charge shows up. So pushing all the risk onto them is both unfair and bad for adoption, because people won't hand over real spending authority if every mistake is on them.

So I think it has to be shared between the agent provider and the payment infrastructure. The agent provider is responsible for the agent behaving within the scope it was given, and for things like prompt injection and misinterpretation. That's a product quality problem, and they should own it the same way a bank owns it when their app has a bug. And then the payment rails need to evolve to actually represent delegated authority. Right now an agent paying on your behalf looks exactly like you paying, which is the whole problem. If the network can see that this was an agent transaction, with these constraints, from this provider, then you can build real dispute processes around it instead of just stuffing it into existing chargeback categories.

The practical thing I'd tell anyone building this today is to make the authorization explicit and narrow. Scoped budgets, merchant allowlists, confirmation for anything above a threshold. Not because it's elegant, but because it makes the question of "who's at fault" answerable after the fact. The failures that are really hard are the ones where the agent did something that was technically in scope but obviously not what the person meant. And I don't think anyone has a clean answer for that yet. That's going to get worked out through a combination of litigation, regulation, and vendors deciding to eat losses to build trust, which is more or less how every previous payment innovation got sorted out too.

r001.rationale: The response says the agent provider should own failures in the agent’s behavior and frames shifting risk away from users as important for adoption and trust.

r002.rationale: It says scoped budgets, allowlists, and confirmations help, but leaves hard cases—such as actions technically in scope but contrary to the user’s intent—without a clean answer.

astra-6.text:
I think the risk should sit with whoever is best positioned to control it. If I authorize an agent to spend up to a hundred dollars on something and it spends a thousand, that shouldn’t be my problem. The system that was supposed to enforce that limit should bear responsibility.

But there’s a harder case where the agent stays within the rules and buys something I didn’t actually want. Was my instruction ambiguous? Did the agent make an unreasonable interpretation? I think you need a clear agreement about what you’re delegating, what requires confirmation, and what happens when something goes wrong.

So I’d start with narrow permissions, spending limits, and the ability to reverse transactions. You can expand the agent’s authority as you build trust. If the starting point is that the user absorbs every mistake, it’s going to be very hard to get people comfortable delegating payments.

r001.rationale: The response assigns responsibility to the system that failed to enforce a spending limit, but it does not identify a payment provider’s accountability as a source of trust.

r002.rationale: It describes a harder case where the agent follows the rules but buys something unwanted, leaving uncertainty about the instruction and the agent’s interpretation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the risk should sit with whoever has the ability to control it. If I explicitly authorize an agent to buy something for a hundred dollars, and it does exactly that, then that’s my purchase. But if it spends a thousand dollars, or pays the wrong person, I don’t think you can just say, well, you gave the agent access, so that’s on you.

You need a clear boundary around what the user authorized, and then a way to verify that the payment stayed within that boundary. The company providing the agent and the payment provider both have a role in enforcing those limits. And when something goes wrong, there needs to be a straightforward way to dispute it. Otherwise, you’re asking people to accept a potentially open-ended liability just to use the product.

r001.rationale: The response gives the payment provider a role in enforcing limits and says disputes should be straightforward, but it does not identify holding the provider accountable for agent mistakes as a source of trust.

r002.rationale: The response describes limits and verification as safeguards while acknowledging that things can still go wrong and require a dispute, communicating residual risk despite those measures.
